GOOGLE OAUTH VERIFICATION SURFACE — iGrowFast LLC

HEADLINE: The Service Account architecture is the single most valuable compliance asset the product has. It mechanically removes iGrowFast from the OAuth verification and CASA surface entirely. Guard it. The website requirements below are cheap; the thing that costs five figures a year is a "Connect your Google account" button, and they do not have one. Do not add one.

=====================================================================
1. GOOGLE API SERVICES USER DATA POLICY
Source: https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy
Workspace overlay: https://developers.google.com/workspace/workspace-api-user-data-developer-policy

DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS (verbatim):
- "publish a privacy policy that fully documents how your application interacts with user data" and list that URL in the OAuth configuration.
- "Your Privacy Policy and all in-product privacy notifications should be accurate, comprehensive, and easily accessible."
- Disclosures must be "prominent and timely."
- Must "accurately represent" three things: who requests the data, what data is requested, why it is requested.
- If data uses expand beyond original disclosures: "update your privacy policy and prompt the user to consent to any changes."
- Minimum scope: "Don't request access to information that you don't need. Only request access to the permissions necessary to implement your application's features."

LIMITED USE — the four obligations (verbatim):
(a) "Limit your use of data to providing or improving user-facing features that are prominent in the requesting application's user interface."
(b) "Transfers of data are not allowed, except: To provide or improve your appropriate access or user-facing features that are visible and prominent in the requesting application's user interface and only with the user's consent; For security purposes (for example, investigating abuse); To comply with applicable laws; or, As part of a merger, acquisition, or sale of assets of the developer after obtaining explicit prior consent from the user."
(c) "Don't allow humans to read the data, unless: You first obtained the user's affirmative agreement to view specific messages, files, or other data...; It is necessary for security purposes...; It is necessary to comply with applicable law; or The data (including derivations) is aggregated and used for internal operations in accordance with applicable privacy and other jurisdictional legal requirements."
(d) Prohibited: "Transferring or selling user data to third parties like advertising platforms, data brokers, or any information resellers"; "Transferring, selling, or using user data for serving ads, including retargeting, personalized or interest-based advertising"; "Transferring, selling, or using user data to determine credit-worthiness or for lending purposes."

*** THE AI/ML QUESTION — DEFINITIVE ANSWER ***
The AI/ML clause is REAL and is in the Workspace API User Data and Developer Policy, verbatim:

  "Transferring, selling, or using user data to create, train, or improve a machine learning or artificial intelligence model beyond that specific user's personalized model for the appropriate use case or user-facing feature."

(Note: two independent summarization passes of the base policy page reported "no AI/ML language exists." That is WRONG — the clause lives in the Workspace overlay policy, which is the one that governs Sheets. Anyone researching this who only reads the base policy will reach the wrong conclusion.)

Does Limited Use prohibit sending Google-user-data to OpenAI/Anthropic? NO — NOT CATEGORICALLY. It draws a hard line between TRAINING and INFERENCE:

- TRAINING on Google user data → PROHIBITED outright, except a model personalized to that specific user for that specific feature. A cross-tenant model trained on many sellers' Sheets data = violation. No consent cures this; it is not one of the enumerated exceptions.
- INFERENCE (sending data to an LLM to produce output for the user) → this is a "transfer to a third party" and is PERMITTED ONLY inside exception (b): the feature must be "visible and prominent in the requesting application's user interface" AND have "the user's consent." A background/invisible AI enrichment pass over Sheets data fails the "prominent in the UI" test.

Therefore three conditions must ALL hold to send Sheets-sourced data to OpenAI/Anthropic:
  1. Zero-retention / no-training API tier, contractually confirmed (both OpenAI and Anthropic API defaults do not train on API data; the retention window and abuse-monitoring human review are the exposure).
  2. The AI feature is prominent and visible in the app UI, not a silent backend process.
  3. Seller consent is obtained and the privacy policy discloses the AI subprocessor by name.
Condition (c) "don't allow humans to read the data" is the sleeper risk: AI-provider trust-and-safety staff reviewing flagged prompts would breach this. Zero-data-retention endpoints are the mitigation.

*** CRITICAL SCOPING INSIGHT — the escape hatch ***
Limited Use governs ONLY data obtained THROUGH Google APIs. COD order data that a seller types directly into iGrowFast, or imports by CSV, is NOT Google user data and Limited Use does not touch it at all. Only the Sheets-sync path is constrained. Architecturally: keep AI features on the native data path, and they are entirely outside this policy. If AI must touch Sheets-sourced rows, the three conditions above bind. This distinction is worth designing around — it is the difference between a governed and an ungoverned AI roadmap.

Compliance with this policy is INDEPENDENT of verification status: per https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464323, all apps must comply with the API Services User Data Policy regardless of whether they are exempt from verification. The Service Account exemption removes the verification process, NOT the Limited Use obligations.

=====================================================================
2. OAUTH APP VERIFICATION
Sources: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463073 ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification

TRIGGER (verbatim): "Apps that request access to scopes categorized as sensitive or restricted must complete Google's OAuth app verification before being granted access." Non-sensitive-only apps are not required to verify (but still need brand verification to show a name/logo on the consent screen). Tier is auto-labelled in the Cloud Console scope picker when you add a scope — the Console is the authoritative tier oracle.

HOMEPAGE (verbatim):
- "The homepage must be hosted on a verified domain you own"
- "The homepage must accurately represent and identify your app or brand"
- "The homepage must describe your app's functionality to its users. Your homepage can not be only a login page"
- "publicly accessible, and not just accessible to your site's logged-in users"
- Must not be a Google Play Store or Facebook page link
- "You must add the link of your privacy policy to your homepage and this link should match the link you added on your OAuth consent screen configuration"

PRIVACY POLICY (verbatim):
- "The Privacy Policy should be hosted within the domain that hosts your homepage" — SAME DOMAIN AS HOMEPAGE, MANDATORY
- "The Privacy Policy should be linked on your homepage so that users can find this information easily"
- "The Privacy Policy must be linked from the OAuth consent screen on the Google API Console"
- "must disclose how your app accesses, uses, stores, and/or shares Google user data"
- "In-product privacy notifications must be prominently displayed in your app interface"

TERMS OF SERVICE: ToS URL is an authorized-domain-listed URI. Google's brand-verification requirements enumerate homepage, privacy policy, ToS, redirect URIs and JS origins as URIs whose top-level domains must all be listed in Authorized Domains and owned/verified. Google specifies far less normative detail for ToS than for the privacy policy — ToS is not the load-bearing document here. UNCERTAIN whether Google mandates a ToS at all for a non-Marketplace OAuth app; it is required as a field for Marketplace listings.

APP NAME / LOGO / BRANDING (verbatim):
- "All apps that access Google APIs must verify that they accurately represent their identity and intent"
- Consent screen must accurately display the app name and logo as configured on the Branding page; "Any changes require resubmission and approval before taking effect."
- "Buttons or links that initiate an action on a Google product must follow the Google branding guidelines."

DEMO VIDEO (required for sensitive/restricted scopes) (verbatim):
- "Show the end-to-end flow of your app including the OAuth grant process"
- "Show the same application you have submitted for verification (including app name, branding)"
- "Show the complete OAuth Consent Screen... The consent screen must also show the same exact scopes you are requesting"
- "Must demonstrate the app functionalities that utilize the requested OAuth scopes"
Practical note for iGrowFast: the video must show the OAuth consent screen with matching branding. It does NOT require a founder on camera or any named person — a screen recording satisfies it. The founder-anonymity constraint is compatible with verification.

3. SCOPE TIERS
Source (authoritative, tier-labelled): https://developers.google.com/sheets/api/scopes ; https://developers.google.com/drive/api/guides/api-specific-auth

Definitions: Non-sensitive = "provide the smallest scope of authorization access"; Sensitive = "provide access to specific Google User Data"; Restricted = "provide wide access to Google User Data."

GOOGLE SHEETS (confirmed tiers):
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets            → SENSITIVE
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets.readonly   → SENSITIVE
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file              → NON-SENSITIVE  ← recommended
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive                   → RESTRICTED     ← triggers CASA
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.readonly          → RESTRICTED     ← triggers CASA

GOOGLE DRIVE (confirmed):
  drive.file, drive.appdata → NON-SENSITIVE ("recommended for most use cases", "per-file access")
  drive, drive.readonly, drive.metadata → RESTRICTED
Google explicitly pushes migration to drive.file, which "grants per-file and narrow access" and avoids the restricted-scope verification burden.

Separately, the Google Ads API imposes its OWN gate independent of OAuth verification: a developer token with Basic/Standard access, approved by a Google Ads API application review. That is a distinct process from OAuth verification and applies regardless.

4. CASA (Cloud Application Security Assessment)
Sources: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13465431 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification ; https://appdefensealliance.dev/casa

WHEN REQUIRED (verbatim): "Every app that requests access to Google users' restricted data and has the ability to access data from or through a third-party server must go through a security assessment."
TIER THAT TRIGGERS IT: RESTRICTED SCOPES ONLY. Sensitive scopes do NOT trigger CASA — they trigger verification (video, homepage, privacy policy) but no security assessment. This is the single most important cost boundary in this whole document.

FRAMEWORK: "To standardize our security assessment we use the App Defense Alliance and the cloud application security assessment framework (CASA)." "CASA utilizes a risk-based, multi-tiered approach"; apps are assigned "either the AL1 or AL2 assurance level." CASA is "based 100% on the OWASP ASVS; no proprietary requirements." Tier assignment is driven by data sensitivity, number of users per data type, risk tolerance, and risk indicators. "All requirements must be satisfied for every level, the only difference between each level is the assessment method that applies."

WHO PERFORMS IT: independent CASA-authorized labs/assessors accredited by the App Defense Alliance. Google does not perform it.

COST: Google's own statement (verbatim, https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817): "Google does not charge the developer any fees for security assessment" and "The cost for such a service is agreed on between the developer and the assessor without any involvement from Google."
UNCERTAIN — DOLLAR FIGURES: A search-engine synthesis surfaced "$500 to $4,500 USD" with "2-3 weeks for tier-2, 4-6 weeks for tier-3," attributed to Google Workspace Marketplace docs. I fetched both Marketplace pages directly (developers.google.com/gsuite/marketplace/security-assessment and /workspace/marketplace/about-app-review) and NEITHER contains those figures — they only say "If your app uses restricted scopes, it must also go through a security assessment." I therefore do NOT assert that range. The older widely-circulated "$15,000–$75,000" figure likewise does not appear in current official documentation. TREAT ALL PUBLISHED DOLLAR FIGURES AS UNVERIFIED; the only official position is that price is negotiated bilaterally with the assessor. Get direct quotes from multiple authorized labs.

FREQUENCY (verbatim): "All applications must be revalidated every year." And: "apps must be reverified for compliance and complete a security assessment at least every 12 months after your assessor's Letter of Assessment (LOA) approval date." "The required assurance level is dynamic and may increase based on changes in your user base or data-handling practices" — i.e. growth alone can escalate the tier.
No free/self-service assessment tier is documented; both AL1 and AL2 are described as lab-tested/lab-verified.

HOW TO AVOID CASA — three independent routes, any one suffices:
  (i) Never request a restricted scope. Use drive.file (non-sensitive) or spreadsheets (sensitive). CASA is restricted-only.
  (ii) Use a Service Account and no user OAuth (see §5) — removes the verification surface entirely.
  (iii) Stay internal-only / under the exemptions in §5.
For iGrowFast, (i) and (ii) both already hold. They are not near CASA and should never go near it.

=====================================================================
5. *** THE CRITICAL ARCHITECTURE QUESTION — SERVICE ACCOUNT ***
Source: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464323 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817

THE EXEMPTION, VERBATIM (Google lists five cases where verification is NOT needed):
  1. "If the app is for your personal use (fewer than 100 users)"
  2. "Apps in development/testing/staging mode are not subject to verification."
  3. "The app only accesses its own data (using a Service Account), and not user data (linked to a Google Account)."
  4. "The app is only used by people in your Google Workspace or Cloud Identity organization" (internal user type)
  5. Workspace admin-trusted / Marketplace apps: "An administrator can add a third-party app to the list of trusted apps in the Google Admin console."

And verbatim from the restricted-scope verification page: "If your app uses a service account to access only its own data, and it doesn't access any user data (linked to a Google Account), then you don't need to submit for verification."

ANSWER: YES — the Service Account model avoids OAuth verification and CASA. But the reasoning that makes it robust is MECHANICAL, not merely textual, and the textual exemption is a weaker support than it first appears. Both halves matter:

THE MECHANICAL ARGUMENT (strong, and the one to rely on):
OAuth verification is a property of the OAuth CLIENT and its CONSENT SCREEN. A service account authenticates as ITSELF via a signed JWT assertion exchanged for a token bearing the SA's own identity. There is no consent screen, no user OAuth grant, no per-user token. Consequently:
  - The "unverified app" warning screen cannot render — there is no consent screen to prepend it to.
  - The 100-new-user cap cannot be consumed — that counter increments on user OAuth grants, of which there are zero.
  - There is no verification submission to make — Google's verification intake is bound to an OAuth consent screen / brand configuration. A product with no consent screen has nothing to submit.
CASA follows verification. No verification surface → no CASA. This holds regardless of which scopes the SA requests: an SA using the Sensitive `spreadsheets` scope still shows no consent screen, so scope tier is moot in the SA path. Tier only starts mattering the moment a consent screen exists.

THE TEXTUAL TENSION (be honest about this — it is the residual risk):
The exemption says "accesses its own data ... and NOT user data (linked to a Google Account)." When a Moroccan seller shares a spreadsheet they OWN with the SA's email, that spreadsheet IS data linked to a Google Account. A literal reading of the exemption is therefore ADVERSE — the SA is a Drive ACL grantee, not the owner. Google's drafting plainly contemplates the canonical case (SA owns/created the resource, e.g. its own BigQuery data), not the shared-file case.
Weighing it: the mechanical argument dominates in practice — Google has no enforcement mechanism against a consent-screen-less SA, and Google's own FAQ blesses an adjacent shared-resource pattern verbatim: "You can access data from your users' Google Cloud projects by creating a service account to represent your service, and then having your customers grant that service account appropriate access to their cloud data using IAM policies." That is precisely the share-with-the-SA topology, described approvingly. This is the strongest available authority for the pattern.
Verdict: the SA + user-shared-sheet model does not require verification and does not incur CASA. Confidence: high on the mechanics, moderate on the letter of the exemption. This is not a five-figure annual assessment — it is nothing.

LIMITS OF THE APPROACH — what breaks it:
  a) DOMAIN-WIDE DELEGATION IS THE TRAP. If the SA is ever given DWD to impersonate users, it IS accessing user data on their behalf and verification applies for sensitive/restricted scopes. DWD is also unusable for iGrowFast's actual users: DWD requires a Google Workspace/Cloud Identity org admin. Sellers on consumer @gmail.com cannot grant it. The manual-share model is not merely acceptable — it is the ONLY option for consumer-Gmail sellers. Fortunate accident: the architecture is forced into the exempt shape.
  b) ADDING A "CONNECT YOUR GOOGLE ACCOUNT" BUTTON destroys the exemption instantly. Per-user OAuth to `spreadsheets` (Sensitive) → full verification: homepage, same-domain privacy policy, demo video, Google review. Still no CASA (Sensitive ≠ Restricted) — unless someone reaches for `drive`/`drive.readonly`, which is Restricted and lands them in annual CASA. Treat a Google-account-connect button as a change requiring explicit sign-off.
  c) LIMITED USE STILL BINDS. The exemption removes the PROCESS, not the POLICY. §1's AI/ML and transfer rules apply to Sheets-sourced data whether or not verification was ever required.
  d) UX/OPERATIONAL COST: sellers must manually share each sheet with an unfriendly SA address (…iam.gserviceaccount.com). Support burden, not a compliance one.
  e) SCOPE MECHANICS: `drive.file` covers only files the app created or the user opened via Picker — it does NOT cover a file manually shared with the SA. For the SA + shared-sheet flow the SA needs `spreadsheets`. Fine (no consent screen), but note this forecloses the "just use drive.file" answer IF they ever migrate to per-user OAuth. On that migration path they'd need `spreadsheets` (Sensitive, verification, no CASA) or a Picker-based drive.file flow (Non-sensitive, no verification) — the Picker route is the one to design toward if they ever leave the SA model.
  f) KEY MANAGEMENT: the SA private key in Postgres Vault is now a crown-jewel credential granting access to every seller sheet ever shared with it. Compromise = cross-tenant breach of end-customer COD data with no per-user revocation granularity (sellers can individually unshare, but there is no token-revocation story). This is the real risk the SA model creates in exchange for the compliance relief. It is a GDPR/security exposure, not a Google-policy one — and given German-hosted infra processing EU-adjacent and Moroccan end-customer PII, it deserves separate attention.

=====================================================================
6. DOMAIN VERIFICATION
Source: https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321

- "You must verify that you own all domains listed in your Authorized domains section."
- Method: "Verify the ownership of your authorized domains using Google Search Console." An account listed as project owner or editor on the GCP project must perform the verification; a Google Account with owner permissions must be associated with the API Console project.
- Authorized Domains must list the top-level domains of every URI: homepage, privacy policy, ToS, redirect URIs, JavaScript origins.

APEX vs SUBDOMAIN — DIRECT ANSWER: verifying the apex is sufficient and subdomains need no separate verification. Google requires verification of "the top private domain" (the domain available for registration on a public suffix). Google's own example, verbatim: "an OAuth consent screen that's configured with an application home page of https://sub.example.com/product asks the account holder to verify ownership of the example.com domain."
For iGrowFast: verify igrowfast.com in Search Console once. That single verification covers app.igrowfast.com and api.igrowfast.com. Homepage on the apex + app on the subdomain is exactly the topology Google's example describes. No conflict.
Founder-anonymity note: Search Console verification is a private control-proof (DNS TXT record or file upload) between the domain owner and Google. It publishes nothing and requires no public name. DNS TXT is the cleanest method. Compatible with the no-founder-names constraint.

=====================================================================
7. CONSEQUENCES OF AN UNVERIFIED APP
Source: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/7454865 ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817

- UNVERIFIED APP SCREEN: shown before the consent screen when the app uses sensitive/restricted scopes and has not completed verification.
- 100-USER CAP (verbatim): "New user cap" of "100 new users in total, after the app presents the unverified app screen." And: "the user cap applies over the entire lifetime of the project, and it cannot be reset or changed." This is lifetime and permanent — not a rolling or resettable quota. Burning it on testing is unrecoverable without a new GCP project.
- HARD FAILURE (verbatim): "Failure to get your app verified before making requests to sensitive or restricted scopes will result in your project's 100 new-user cap eventually getting exhausted and Google sign-in being disabled for your users."
- ADDITIONAL SIGNALS: Google Security Checkup flags the app as "risky and unverified"; users get notices about potential loss of functionality.
- GRACE PERIOD: exists only in one narrow case — when Google RECLASSIFIES a scope as sensitive/restricted, existing apps get "a grace period to go through verification before the unverified app screen and user cap are applied." There is no general grace period for new apps.
- RESTRICTED SCOPES: not described as an instant hard block; they route through the same warning + cap mechanism, plus the mandatory security assessment before verification can complete.
- Testing/dev is explicitly fine unverified: you can "continue to build and test your app while waiting to complete verification."

ALL OF §7 IS INAPPLICABLE TO THE SA PATH — these consequences attach to the OAuth consent screen, which the SA architecture does not have. §7 is the description of what iGrowFast is avoiding, and the reason to keep avoiding it.

=====================================================================
NET ASSESSMENT FOR iGrowFast
- Today, on the Service Account model: NO OAuth verification, NO CASA, NO 100-user cap, NO demo video. Zero Google review exposure.
- The website requirements (homepage, same-domain privacy policy, Search Console verification) are NOT currently mandatory for Google, because nothing triggers verification. Build them anyway — they are cheap, they are required by GDPR/Moroccan reality independent of Google, and they are the prerequisite that must already exist on the day anyone proposes a Google-account-connect button. Retrofitting them under deadline is where projects fail.
- The live, binding Google obligation today is LIMITED USE on Sheets-sourced data — specifically the prohibition on training AI/ML models on it. This constrains the AI roadmap NOW, with no verification trigger and no warning shot.
- Highest-leverage decisions: (1) never request drive/drive.readonly; (2) never add per-user OAuth without deliberate sign-off; (3) never enable domain-wide delegation; (4) keep AI features on the native (non-Sheets) data path where Limited Use does not reach; (5) treat the SA key as the cross-tenant crown jewel it now is.
- Two open items: exact Console tier labels for analytics/adwords scopes (confirm in the Cloud Console scope picker — it auto-labels), and real CASA pricing (only if they ever go restricted, which they should not).

## HEADLINE

Two 2026 developments invalidate most published guidance on this topic. Report them as the current state:

1. **FISA §702 lapsed 12 June 2026** (EFF: "The authority for this program is set to expire Friday, June 12th, 2026, at midnight" — https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/victory-702-has-expired). Brennan Center notes collection continues under existing certifications until ~March 2027 regardless ("Section 702 Surveillance Will Continue Until March 2027 Even if the Statute Lapses" — https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/section-702-foreign-intelligence-surveillance-act-fisa-2026-resource-page).
2. **Trump v. Slaughter (US Supreme Court, 29 June 2026)** — President may remove FTC commissioners at will. The DPF adequacy decision leans on FTC independence (noyb counts 259 references). noyb demands withdrawal and plans a CJEU annulment action (https://noyb.eu/en/us-supreme-court-just-blew-eu-us-data-transfers). Commission says it is analysing implications; **the adequacy decision remains formally in force** — Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 is valid until repealed by the Commission or annulled by the Union courts.

Honest balance, not the alarmist read: IAPP publishes a credible counter-argument that Slaughter does **not** undo the redress mechanism — it constrains *congressional* limits on removal, not a President binding himself; the DPRC rests on EO 14086 self-binding; DPRC judges are "inferior officers" under Morrison v. Olson; and the Court expressly declined to decide consequences for adjudicators (https://iapp.org/news/a/no-trump-v-slaughter-does-not-undo-the-eu-us-data-transfer-redress-mechanism). What is hit is the **FTC commercial-supervision leg**, which is precisely the leg GA transfers ride on. Net: DPF is lawful to rely on **today**, with a materially elevated probability of disruption in 12–24 months.

## 1. GA TERMS OF SERVICE — THE ACTUAL OBLIGATION

US ToS, effective 15 May 2023 (https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/us/), §7 Privacy — verbatim:
- "You will have and abide by an appropriate Privacy Policy and will comply with all applicable laws, policies, and regulations relating to the collection of information from Users."
- "You must post a Privacy Policy and that Privacy Policy must provide notice of Your use of cookies, identifiers for mobile devices (e.g., Android Advertising Identifier or Advertising Identifier for iOS) or similar technology used to collect data."
- "You must disclose the use of Google Analytics, and how it collects and processes data." Satisfiable "by displaying a prominent link to the site 'How Google uses information from sites or apps that use our services'" (https://policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites).
- **PII prohibition:** "You will not and will not assist or permit any third party to pass information, hashed or otherwise, to Google that Google could use or recognize as personally identifiable information."

EU/UK ToS, effective 11 January 2024 (https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/gb/) adds a clause the US version lacks: "You will use commercially reasonable efforts to ensure that a User is provided with clear and comprehensive information about, and consents to, the storing and accessing of cookies." It also incorporates the Google Ads Data Processing Terms (https://business.safety.google/adsprocessorterms/).

**The PII clause is the sharpest edge for this entity.** iGrowFast processes end-customer names, phones, delivery addresses, order contents. Putting GA on **app.igrowfast.com** would risk order IDs/phones/addresses reaching Google in page paths, titles, or query params — a direct §7 breach, and Google's remedy is account termination and data deletion. This is an own-goal risk that a COD product does not need to take.

## 2. CONSENT MODE V2 — MANDATORY, BUT NOT AS LAW

Not a legal obligation. It is a **Google contractual/technical requirement**, enforced by feature degradation, not fines.
- Binding instrument is the **EU User Consent Policy** (https://www.google.com/about/company/user-consent-policy/): obtain "legally valid consent to: the use of cookies or other local storage where legally required; and the collection, sharing, and use of personal data for personalization of ads"; "clearly identify each party that may collect, receive, or use end users' personal data"; retain consent records; provide revocation instructions. Scope: EEA, UK, Switzerland.
- Required since **March 2024** for EEA/UK traffic where Google tags/SDKs are used (https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13695607). Four signals: `ad_storage`, `analytics_storage`, `ad_user_data`, `ad_personalization`.
- **Enforcement mechanism = capability loss, not penalty.** Google Analytics help states plainly: "If you don't send consent signals, you will lose ads personalization capabilities" (https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/14009343). Audiences stop populating, remarketing lists die, conversion modeling is disabled. Google does not fine you; it degrades you.
- **NEW — 15 June 2026** (https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/17016975): "Google Analytics will transition to using Consent Mode (within Google Ads) as the single control for data." Previously collection was governed by *both* the Google Signals setting *and* Consent Mode Ads settings; that duality is removed. Google Signals "will only control the association of your Google Analytics sourced data with signed in user information for behavioral reporting."

**Applied to iGrowFast:** a pure marketing site with no Google Ads and no remarketing has nothing to lose from omitting Consent Mode v2 — the enforcement is loss of ad features you aren't using. It becomes required the moment iGrowFast runs Google Ads (likely for a COD/e-commerce vendor). This is a strong argument for keeping GA off the marketing site *now* and adding GTM + a certified CMP + Consent Mode v2 later, scoped to conversion tracking only, if and when paid acquisition starts.

## 3. EU COOKIE CONSENT — WHAT MUST HAPPEN BEFORE THE TAG FIRES

Legal basis is **ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3)**, not GDPR: prior consent before any non-essential storage or access on terminal equipment. GA4 writes `_ga` cookies → **consent must be obtained BEFORE the tag fires.** Consent Mode's `denied` default is a mitigation for Google's contract, not an exemption from Art. 5(3).

**EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce Report, adopted 17 January 2023** (https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2023-01/edpb_20230118_report_cookie_banner_taskforce_en.pdf) — read directly from the PDF:
- **No reject button on first layer (§3):** "a vast majority of authorities considered that the absence of refuse/reject/not consent options on any layer with a consent button is an infringement of the ePrivacy Directive."
- **Pre-ticked boxes (§4, ¶10):** "pre-ticked boxes to opt-in do not lead to valid consent," citing GDPR recital 32 ("Silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent").
- **Deceptive link design (¶11):** a *link* rather than a *button* to reject is called out as deceptive.
- **Deceptive colours/contrast (§6, ¶15–17):** no general standard; case-by-case verification that contrast/colours are not "obviously" misleading.
- **Legitimate interest for analytics (§7, ¶31):** "no overriding legitimate interest would exist for such" processing — LI is not available as a workaround.
- **Withdrawal (§9, ¶31–32):** "as easy to withdraw as to give consent"; controllers must provide easily accessible withdrawal.

**CNIL Sheet n°16** (https://www.cnil.fr/en/sheet-ndeg16-use-analytics-your-websites-and-applications) — an exemption for audience measurement exists, conditioned on: inform + ability to object; strictly audience measurement/A-B testing; "not to cross-check the data processed with other processing"; "to limit the scope of the tracer to a single site or application editor"; "to truncate the last byte of the IP address"; 13-month tracker lifetime (25-month data retention). **CNIL's verdict on GA is explicit: "Most large audience measurement offerings do not fall within the scope of the exemption, regardless of their configuration."** CNIL recommends "open source software such as Matomo that you can configure yourself." **GA4 cannot be made consent-free in France at any configuration.**

**Status of the 2022–23 decisions — the honest answer:** Austria DSB (decided 22 Dec 2021, published 13 Jan 2022), CNIL (10 Feb 2022), Garante (June 2022). All rested on the **Chapter V transfer** leg post-Schrems II — i.e. that no valid transfer mechanism existed. The DPF adequacy decision (10 July 2023) + Google's certification **addresses that specific leg**. The decisions were never "overturned"; they were decided under a legal state that no longer obtains, and are effectively superseded *on transfers only*. **The consent leg is entirely untouched** — GA still requires prior ePrivacy consent whether or not the DPF stands. Anyone claiming "the DPF made Google Analytics legal" is conflating two independent legs. Note also the Garante ban would not require a fresh investigation if the DPF falls.

**DPF litigation posture** (verified against EUR-Lex OJ C/2025/6610, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202506610):
- **Latombe v Commission, T-553/23** — General Court (Tenth Chamber, Extended Composition) dismissed the annulment action **3 September 2025**, ECLI:EU:T:2025:831 (https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2025-09/cp250106en.pdf).
- **Appeal C-703/25 P filed 31 October 2025**, pending. Four grounds; first alleges error re: independence of the Data Protection Review Court under Art. 47 Charter / Art. 45(2) GDPR. Parties: European Commission, Ireland, **United States of America**. Microsoft granted leave to intervene supporting the Commission. No hearing date announced.

## 4. IS GOOGLE DPF-CERTIFIED? — YES, WITH ONE VERIFICATION CAVEAT

Google's own official attestation (https://policies.google.com/privacy/frameworks): "Google LLC (and its wholly-owned US subsidiaries unless explicitly excluded) has certified that it adheres to the DPF Principles" — covering **EU-U.S. DPF, Swiss-U.S. DPF, and the UK Extension**.

Ads/analytics-specific (https://business.safety.google/adsdatatransfers/): "As of 1 September 2023, when our clients and partners use Google's Ads Services, Google relies on the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework" for EEA→US transfers; Swiss-U.S. DPF and UK Extension from 16 September 2024. Google also "may rely on SCCs for certain data transfers in connection with our advertising and analytics products" where DPF does not cover.

**Verification caveat — stated honestly:** I could not independently render the Commerce list record. dataprivacyframework.gov is a client-rendered SPA and its participant API is not publicly reachable (I probed both; returns "resource cannot be displayed"). Google's participant record is at https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/participant/5780 — **confirm Active status in a browser before relying on it in any published document or DPIA.** Do not cite it as verified until someone loads it.

**What it means for GA transfers:** the Chapter V leg is covered by adequacy — no SCCs, no TIA required for the DPF-covered flow. It does **not** cure the ePrivacy consent requirement, does **not** cure the §7 PII prohibition, and does **not** cure Google's own controller-side processing.

## 5. GOOGLE SIGNALS / DATA SHARING — EXTRA DISCLOSURE OBLIGATIONS

**Advertising Features Policy** (https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2700409) — you must disclose, verbatim:
1. "The Google Analytics Advertising Features you've implemented."
2. "How you and third-party vendors use first-party cookies (such as the Google Analytics cookie) or other first-party identifiers, and third-party cookies (such as Google advertising cookies) or other third-party identifiers together."
3. "How visitors can opt-out of the Google Analytics Advertising Features you use, including through Ads Settings, Ad Settings for mobile apps, or any other available means."
Plus: "you will not identify users or facilitate the merging of personally identifiable information with additional information collected through any Google advertising product or feature unless you have robust notice of, and the user's prior affirmative (i.e., opt-in) consent."

**The role flip — this is the important one.** Enabling the Data Sharing Setting ("Google products & services") + accepting the **Measurement Controller-Controller Data Protection Terms** makes **Google an independent controller**, not your processor (https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9012600). Verbatim: each party "is an independent controller of Controller Personal Data; [and] will individually determine the purposes and means of its processing of Controller Personal Data." And the burden shifts to you: "Customer will comply with the Policies in relation to the Controller Personal Data shared pursuant to the Data Sharing Setting and **at all times will bear the burden of proof in establishing such compliance**." "Policies" = the Google End User Consent Policy. Transfers reference Controller SCCs unless an "Alternative Transfer Solution" (i.e. DPF) is adopted.

**Recommendation: Google Signals OFF, data sharing OFF.** It avoids the controller-controller terms, the burden-of-proof clause, the three extra disclosures, and the 15 June 2026 transition entirely.

## 6. ALTERNATIVES — RECOMMENDATION: CLOUDFLARE WEB ANALYTICS

**Recommend Cloudflare Web Analytics for igrowfast.com. Do not put GA4 on the marketing site.**

Reasoning, weighted to the real facts:
- **It is genuinely cookieless.** Cloudflare, verbatim: "We don't use any client-side state (like cookies or localStorage) for analytics purposes" (https://blog.cloudflare.com/privacy-first-web-analytics/). It also refuses fingerprinting via IP/User-Agent, calling it "even more intrusive than cookies, because users have no way to opt out." Counts visits via referrer rather than per-user identifiers.
- **No cookie → Art. 5(3) ePrivacy is not engaged → no consent banner.** That single fact deletes the entire EDPB banner surface (reject-button parity, pre-ticked boxes, colour/contrast, withdrawal UI), all of Consent Mode v2, the GA ToS privacy-notice and PII obligations, and the whole DPF-transfer narrative from the marketing site. Be precise: server-side IP handling is still GDPR processing → you still need a privacy notice and a legal basis (legitimate interest), just not a consent gate.
- **Zero marginal cost and zero new vendor.** Free on all plans, and the site sits behind Cloudflare already — no DNS change, no new sub-processor, no new DPA.
- **It removes the PII own-goal.** No Google tag on a COD property means no path for customer phone numbers or addresses to leak to Google via URLs and breach GA ToS §7.
- **The stated need is modest.** Pageviews, referrers, top pages, and country. Cloudflare covers that. GA4's value is ads attribution and audiences — precisely the features iGrowFast is not using on a marketing site today.
- **Optionality is preserved.** If paid acquisition starts, add GTM + a Google-certified CMP + Consent Mode v2 at that point, consent-gated, scoped to conversion only, Signals off.

Alternatives considered and why they lose: **self-hosted Matomo** is the CNIL-blessed option (explicitly named in Sheet n°16) and is the only route to a *consent-exempt* analytics posture that CNIL has endorsed by name — but it adds ops burden to VPSs already carrying the app, for a marketing site. **Plausible** is EU-hosted and cookieless but paid and adds a vendor for no gain over Cloudflare here. If the exemption posture ever needs to be defensible to CNIL specifically, Matomo self-hosted on the existing German boxes is the upgrade path.

**Territorial-scope honesty:** GDPR exposure here is real but modest and arguable. Users are Morocco-centric; the German Contabo VPSs are infrastructure and do not by themselves create an Art. 3(1) establishment; Art. 3(2) bites only insofar as the site targets EU sellers (positioning says "worldwide"). This does not change the recommendation — the banner-free path costs nothing and needs no scope argument. Separately and out of scope but flagged: Morocco's **Law 09-08 / CNDP** is plausibly a more operative regime for the app's end-customer data than GDPR is, and nobody appears to have assessed it.

## 7. THE PRODUCT'S GA USAGE — MULTI-TENANT OBLIGATIONS

**Serving a client's own GA data to that client's own staff is permitted**, and the allow-list model is the correct control. Specifics:

- **Google API Services User Data Policy** (https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy) — Limited Use: "Limit your use of data to providing or improving user-facing features that are prominent in the requesting application's user interface." Transfers "are not allowed, except: To provide or improve your appropriate access or user-facing features...only with the user's consent; For security purposes; To comply with applicable laws; or As part of a merger, acquisition, or sale." Prohibits "Transferring or selling user data to third parties like advertising platforms, data brokers, or any information resellers" and using data "for serving ads, including retargeting, personalized or interest-based advertising." Requires "a privacy policy that fully documents how your application interacts with user data."
  → A per-media-buyer GA view **is** a prominent user-facing feature = compliant. Showing Client A's GA data to Client B's staff would breach Limited Use. **The allow-list is therefore ToS-load-bearing, not merely a product nicety.**

- **The Service-Account-in-Vault pattern is the real risk.** A service account added to each client's GA property works, but it bypasses per-user OAuth consent and becomes a **cross-tenant master key**: anything able to query through it can read every linked property. Google enforces nothing here — the allow-list is enforced in *your* app. An allow-list bug is a cross-tenant data breach and a ToS breach simultaneously. This is structurally the same failure mode as the RLS cross-tenant issues already in this project's history. It warrants the same adversarial treatment: default-deny, scope resolved server-side, never trust a client-supplied property ID.

- **Client must accept GA ToS itself, and must expressly consent to your access.** Provisioning API Program Agreement (https://developers.google.com/analytics/terms/provisioning/en): "All promotion of Google Analytics by Company to Customers must require Customers to sign up for Google Analytics in accordance with the applicable Google Analytics terms and conditions"; Company is prohibited from "accessing Customer's Google Analytics account or data unless Company has Customer's express consent to do so."
  **Precision — do not conflate two APIs:** that agreement's "Company may only use the Provisioning API for internal use cases; Provisioning API may not be used to create publicly available applications" restricts the **Provisioning API** (account creation). Reading GA data via the **GA4 Data API** is a different surface and is *not* subject to that internal-use-only clause. Several secondary sources get this wrong.

- **Quotas are not a problem** (https://developers.google.com/analytics/devguides/reporting/data/v1/quotas). Standard properties: Core Tokens Per Property Per Day 200,000; Per Property Per Hour 40,000; **Per Project Per Property Per Hour 14,000**; Core Concurrent Requests Per Property 10. Analytics 360 = 10× each (2,000,000 / 400,000 / 140,000 / 50). Quotas are scoped **per property**, so multi-tenant access scales naturally — each client property carries its own bucket. Your binding limit is the 14,000 project-per-property-per-hour figure. Google notes "one property must be accessed by more than 3 projects before the 'Tokens Per Property Per Hour' quota could be exhausted before the 'Tokens Per Project Per Property Per Hour' quota." Per-property response caching is the mitigation; there is no multi-tenant quota cliff.

- **GA ToS §9** is relevant if you administer properties for clients: it requires you to represent you are "authorized to bind third parties," and "Google may share with the Third Party any Customer Data that is specific to the Third Party Properties."

**Adjacent gap, flagged not researched:** the Google Sheets sales-channel sync pushes end-customer order data (names, phones, addresses) into Google Sheets. That is a Google API Services User Data Policy surface, a third-country transfer, and a **sub-processor relationship that must appear in the seller-facing DPA/sub-processor list**. It carries more end-customer PII risk than the entire GA question and appears unassessed.

## ENTITY-SPECIFIC NOTES
- Founder names are not required anywhere in a privacy notice or cookie policy — controller identity is satisfied by "iGrowFast LLC, 30 N Gould St Ste R, Sheridan, WY 82801, USA" plus a role contact address. EIN is never required. Neither constraint conflicts with any obligation found.
- If the marketing site targets EU sellers, **GDPR Art. 27 EU representative** is a separate obligation independent of the analytics choice — assess it.
- Recommended posture: apex igrowfast.com → Cloudflare Web Analytics, no banner, privacy notice with LI basis. app.igrowfast.com → **no third-party analytics tags at all**, given the customer-PII payload.

## 1. GOOGLE ADS API ACCESS TIERS

Four tiers, not three ([Access Levels and Permissible Use](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/api-policy/access-levels)):

| Level | Accounts | Ops/day | Review |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Test Account** | test only | 15,000 | auto on signup |
| **Explorer** | test + production | 2,880 (prod) / 15,000 (test) | may be auto-granted after signup |
| **Basic** | test + production | 15,000 | ~5 business days |
| **Standard** | test + production | unlimited (most services) | ~10 business days; requires Basic first |

**Explorer** is restricted from: account creation, user management, keyword planning, audience insights, account billing/payments.

**Application mechanics (NOT a website form — this is a config/filing action):** done in the [API Center](https://ads.google.com/aw/apicenter) of a **Google Ads manager account**. Steps per [Developer Token](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/api-policy/developer-token): complete the API Access form, accept the T&C, then apply for Basic via the Access-level dropdown.

**What Google actually demands about the website — this is the load-bearing part for igrowfast.com:**
- Company name + **company website URL**.
- Verbatim: *"Ensure that your information is correct and your company's website URL is functioning. If the website is not live, Google might not be able to process your application and reject it."*
- Verbatim: *"Generic URLs such as `test.com` and `example.com` are not accepted."*
- Individuals may substitute a GitHub/LinkedIn URL. Not our case — iGrowFast LLC is a company.
- The API contact email **must be a monitored inbox**: *"Google's API compliance team might reach out to this email address during the review process for clarifications."*

Google's public docs do **not** enumerate a checklist of what the site must display. The real gate is: the site must be live, must be the company's, must plausibly describe a real tool that matches the declared permissible use, and must survive a human compliance reviewer. There is no documented requirement to show founder names or EIN — company name + working URL only. Both constraints (no founders, no EIN) are compatible with the application.

**Brand verification of Google Cloud projects** is *"optional and is used only as a signal for faster determination of Ads API Basic Access eligibility."* Config action, not a website item.

**Tool review is real, and it's contractual:** [Google Ads API policies](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6169371) — *"Upon request from Google, you must provide a demo account to your API tool within 7 days of the request."* Must be a live or functionally identical version. Providing a false account is a violation. For Standard: *"If your tool is used by external users, be prepared to provide demo sign-in access to your tool."*

**Permissible use** (applies only to Basic/Standard) — three categories, you declare one:
1. **Ad creation / management** — all services.
2. **Reporting** — restricted to `GoogleAdsService.Search` / `SearchStream`, read-only calls.
3. **Researching keywords and recommendations** — `RecommendationService`, `KeywordPlanIdeaService`, `KeywordPlanService`.

Changing it later = separate "application to update permissible use". **Given the codebase (Google Ads campaign data surfaced to media buyers, no campaign mutation), the correct declaration is Reporting.** That declaration is binding: *"You may only use the API functionality in the way described in your token application."*

**Cloud-managed access levels** ([no-developer-token](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/concepts/no-developer-token)) is a **pilot**, requires an already-approved developer token plus a Google Cloud organization. Not a shortcut. Ignore for now.

## 2. REQUIRED MINIMUM FUNCTIONALITY

[RMF](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/api-policy/rmf). **The decisive fact: *"RMF only applies to developer tokens with Standard Access level."*** At Basic, RMF does not bind.

Tool classification (verbatim):
- **Full-Service Tool** — *"advertisers, agencies, and other third parties use your tool to fully manage their Google Ads accounts"* → Creation + Management + Reporting RMF all apply.
- **Reporting Only** — *"only a reporting dashboard available to end-advertisers"* → **only Reporting RMF applies. Creation and Management RMF do not apply.**
- **Internal Use Only** — *"individual advertiser or agency use only; no third-party access to tool"* → no RMF.

**Direct answer to the question: a reporting-only integration does NOT have to expose campaign creation or management.** Google does not force management capability onto a reporting dashboard. It only forces *completeness of reporting* at whatever hierarchy levels you choose to display: *"Reporting Functionality for each of the levels of the Google Ads hierarchy displayed in its reporting interface."*

Reporting RMF fields, per level:
- **R.10 Customer:** `metrics.clicks`, `metrics.cost_micros`, `metrics.impressions`, `metrics.conversions`, `metrics.all_conversions`
- **R.20 Campaign:** same five, plus campaign status when showing paused/active/removed
- **R.40 Ad Group Ad:** clicks, cost_micros, impressions, conversions
- **R.50 Keyword View:** clicks, cost_micros, impressions, conversions + position estimate data
- **R.70 Search Term View:** `search_term_view.search_term`, `segments.search_term_match_type`, clicks, cost_micros, impressions

No due dates on the base set = already past due (binding immediately at Standard).

**Strategic consequence:** stay at **Basic + Reporting permissible use**. 15,000 ops/day. RMF never triggers, no tool audit against RMF, no obligation to build campaign creation UI. Applying for Standard would drag the whole product into an RMF audit for no benefit unless volume forces it.

**Structural conflict with the existing MB-facing data rule:** the memory rule says MB views hide spend and ROAS. Reporting RMF **mandates `metrics.cost_micros` at every displayed level.** These are incompatible at Standard. At Basic they are not — another reason Standard is the wrong door.

## 3. GOOGLE ADS API TERMS — OBLIGATIONS

[T&C](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/api-policy/terms) + [policies](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6169371).

**Scope lock:** *"You can only use the Google Ads API for Google Ads campaign creation, management, or reporting."*

**Displaying Ads data to third parties — the sharpest issue for our media-buyer model.** Legacy [AdWords API T&C](https://www.google.com/adwords/select/TCNetApi2012-03.html), carried forward in substance: *"you shall not sell, redistribute, sublicense or otherwise disclose or transfer to any Third Party all or any portion of AdWords API Report Data (except that you may disclose the AdWords API Report Data from a particular account to the owner of that account)."* And: the client *"must neither enable nor allow any party to access or use the account, passwords, AdWords API Data or any other account information of a party other than the then-current end-user (**which includes parties acting on an end-user's behalf and authorized by that end-user to do so**), whether or not the AdWords API Data is in identifiable or aggregate form."*

The parenthetical is the escape hatch: media buyers are permissible viewers **only** as authorized agents of the account owner. The existing per-MB allow-list scoping model is what makes this defensible — but it must be *actually enforced server-side* and *authorized by the seller*, not just a UI filter. Aggregation does not launder it ("whether or not ... in aggregate form").

Current policy restates it: *"you must obtain written consent from your clients before selling, redistributing, sub-licensing, or otherwise disclosing or transferring data specific to their Google Ads accounts."*

**Data retention:** there is **no** specific retention/deletion period in the Ads API T&C. The only deletion obligation is at termination (Section 15): stop using the API and *"delete all Google Ads API Specifications in your possession"* — that's the specs, not the data. **Do not invent a retention clause.** The real obligations are security and disassociation:
- *"You must use all reasonable efforts to keep advertisers' Google Ads API data in a secure environment at all times."* Maintained *"according to commonly acceptable security standards."*
- All data transfers require *"at least 128 Bit SSL encryption."*
- **Disassociation right:** *"Within 3 business days of receiving notice from an end-advertiser client, you must provide that client the ability to disassociate."*

**Disclosure to our customers:**
- **24-hour rule:** *"If your reporting of Google Ads performance data is delayed to end-advertisers or other clients by more than 24 hours, you must prominently disclose this delay."* Our sync cadence must be measured; if >24h, this is a **prominent** on-page/in-app disclosure, not a buried ToS line.
- Must disclose platform incompatibilities when offering cross-platform bulk editing (we surface Meta + Google Ads side by side — relevant).
- Google Ads data must be **reported separately from competing platform data** and at the granularity Google Ads offers. Our combined Meta/Google campaign views need to keep Google Ads data separably attributable.
- Must comply with [Google's third-party policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6086450): be *"honest and transparent about your company, services, associated costs, and expected results."*
- [Transparency requirements](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16489093): monthly performance report with cost/clicks/impressions at the Google advertising account level, **or** let customers sign in to their own Google accounts directly. Management fees must be disclosed in writing before first purchase and on all invoices. Must provide customer IDs on request.

**Is there a required "we access your Google Ads account" clause in our Terms?** Not literally worded as such in the Ads API T&C. But it is compelled indirectly and unavoidably: written consent for any onward disclosure (§ MB access), the honesty/transparency duty, and the [Google API Services User Data Policy](https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy) requirement to *"accurately represent"* the app identity, the data requested, and the purpose, with a privacy policy that *"thoroughly disclose[s] how the application accesses, uses, stores, or shares user data."* **Practical verdict: yes — put it in writing.**

**Prohibited practices (verbatim, all directly relevant):**
- *"Your Google Ads API tool may not replicate the look and feel of the Google Ads user interface or otherwise confuse others into believing that your tool is a Google product."*
- *"As a user of the Google Ads API, you must comply with Google's brand-usage guidelines."*
- No requiring end-advertisers to obtain supplemental tokens.
- No providing automated third-party access via **your** token instead of their own.
- No circumventing RMF via secondary APIs.
- Token revoked after **90 consecutive days of inactivity**.
- Non-compliance fees per rate sheet; downgrade or termination.

## 4. BRAND / TRADEMARK — GOOGLE, GOOGLE ADS

Governed by T&C §6 (*"You must only use the Google Brand Features in accordance with (a) these terms and (b) the then current Google Brand Features Use Guidelines"* at google.com/permissions) → [Brand Resource Center](https://about.google/brand-resource-center/guidance/).

**Plain text: ALLOWED, no request needed.** *"You can use Google in plain text and refer to Google or its products in an informational context in plain text in books, articles, websites, etc., as long as you follow Google's Trademark Rules."*

**Logos: NOT allowed without a permission request.** *"Don't use the Google logo in marketing materials for a business or to imply endorsement from Google."* *"Use only Google-approved artwork."* The license is granted only *"for the sole purpose and only for the materials set forth"* in a submitted [Permission Request Form](https://partnermarketinghub.withgoogle.com/brands/google/trademarks-and-terms/terms-and-conditions/) — *"non-transferable, non-exclusive, royalty-free limited license"* — and Google *"reserves the right in its sole discretion to terminate or modify your permission."*

**"Google Ads integration" — permitted**, because it is nominative adjectival use. [Trademark rules](https://partnermarketinghub.withgoogle.com/brands/google/trademarks-and-terms/trademark-guidelines-for-proper-usage/):
- Use as **adjective only** — *"never as a noun, verb, plural, or possessive form."*
- **Follow with the generic term** (e.g., "Google Ads™ advertising platform", "Google Ads™ campaign data").
- Distinguish from surrounding text: capitalize / italicize / quote / different type style.
- Spell exactly as on the trademark list; no alterations, hyphens, abbreviations, acronyms.
- **Never the most prominent element** on the page.
- ® only in countries where registered; ™ otherwise.

**Hard prohibitions:**
- *"No false affiliation: Cannot imply endorsement, sponsorship, or partnership with Google."*
- *"Cannot use, incorporate, or combine any Google trademarks (names or logos) into your brand name, product name, business name, trade name, website domain, or slogan."*
- *"No imitation: Don't copy Google's design aesthetic, colors, typography, or imagery."* — reinforced by the Ads API "look and feel" prohibition.
- No Google marks in social media account names or profiles; no domain registration at any level.
- Prohibited adjacent to adult content, gambling, tobacco/alcohol.

**Required attribution notice:** *"Any use of Google Brand Features must be accompanied by a notice that clearly indicates that the Google Brand Features are trademarks or distinctive brand features of Google LLC."* Google provides a **legal line generator** to auto-generate the correct attribution statement. Practical form: `Google Ads™ is a trademark of Google LLC.`

**Can we imply partnership? No — absolutely not.** Banned strings for igrowfast.com: "Google Partner", "Official Google …", "Powered by Google", "Certified by Google", "Endorsed by Google", "In partnership with Google", any Google logo in a "trusted by / partners" row.

**Google Analytics is the exception and is more permissive** — [Google Analytics Developer Branding Guidelines](https://developers.google.com/analytics/terms/branding-policy):
- Developers **may use GA logos without special approval**, specifically when the app displays Google Analytics data publicly, to non-owners, or commercially. **This describes our product exactly** (GA data surfaced per media-buyer = displayed to non-owners, commercially).
- Approved phrasing: *"Great App for Google Analytics"*, or that your app *"works with Google Analytics."*
- **Cannot** use "Google Analytics" in the app's primary name or description (e.g. not "Google Analytics for Enterprises").
- *"All Google Analytics logos used within an application must link back to Google Analytics"* — product homepage or into the platform. One logo per page suffices.
- Min sizes: horizontal 154×50 px; vertical 132×100 px. Sufficient contrast. Never the most prominent element. No modifying/altering/partially covering.
- Note the scope wording is "within an application" — this policy cleanly covers app.igrowfast.com. For the **marketing site** at igrowfast.com the safer read is the general Brand Resource Center rules (logo → permission request). Text-only on the marketing site is the zero-risk option.

## 5. GOOGLE SHEETS ON THE MARKETING SITE

Two regimes. Our Sheets sync uses a **service account** (per the codebase) — server-to-server, no user OAuth consent screen, not a Marketplace add-on. So [Workspace Marketplace branding guidelines](https://developers.google.com/workspace/marketplace/terms/branding) are not *binding* today, but they are the clearest statement of Google's naming logic and the general Brand Resource Center rules do bind:

- **Naming:** *"Don't use any Google trademarks or any confusingly similar marks as the name of your extension or company."*
- **Permitted construction:** *"for," "for use with," or "compatible with"* before the trademark — e.g. "for Gmail™", "for Google Chat™". So **"for Google Sheets™"** / **"compatible with Google Sheets™"** / **"Google Sheets™ integration"** are all fine.
- **Logo:** *"Do not use Google brand elements or modified versions as your application logo."* The Sheets logo on the marketing site as decoration in an integrations grid = general Brand Resource Center rules = **permission request required**.
- **Screenshots:** *"standard, unaltered screenshots of Google services"* may be used for illustrative purposes, subject to permissions requirements. Useful for an integrations page — but a screenshot of a Sheet must not contain real end-customer PII.
- **Attribution pattern given by Google:** listing "Productivity tool for Google Chat™" + notice "Google Chat™ is a trademark of Google LLC". Mirror exactly: `Google Sheets™ is a trademark of Google LLC.`

**Independent of branding, [Google API Services User Data Policy](https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy) bites now:** accurately represent app identity/data/purpose; published, accurate, comprehensive, easily accessible privacy policy with the URL in the OAuth client config; **minimum scope**; **Limited Use** — data limited to *"providing or improving user-facing features that are prominent"*; and a hard bar: **cannot transfer or sell user data to advertising platforms, data brokers, or information resellers**, and cannot use it for ad serving, credit determination, or lending.

## 6. WORKSPACE MARKETPLACE — FUTURE PATH ONLY

**Flag: future / not currently applicable.** Only relevant if the Sheets sync is ever rebuilt as a user-OAuth add-on and listed publicly. Requirements ([App review process](https://developers.google.com/workspace/marketplace/about-app-review), [Configure OAuth](https://developers.google.com/workspace/marketplace/configure-oauth-consent-screen)):
- Billing enabled on the Google Cloud project.
- **App review**: design, content, functionality, user experience. Common rejections: incomplete OAuth verification, inaccurate app listings, functionality issues.
- **OAuth verification** — a **separate process** from app review, required for public apps using sensitive or restricted scopes. May require a **demo video**.
- **Security assessment** if restricted scopes are requested — **renewed annually** (third-party CASA assessment, material cost).
- Marketplace branding guidelines (§5) become binding on the listing.

Sheets scopes (`spreadsheets`) are *sensitive*, not *restricted* — so OAuth verification yes, annual security assessment likely no. The service-account architecture avoids all of this. **Recommendation: do not go to Marketplace.**

## 7. GOOGLE POLICIES RESTRICTING OUR USE CASES

**Nothing in the Google Ads API prohibits COD, dropshipping, or automated messaging.** No such clause exists. Do not let anyone claim otherwise. The API's only use restriction is the scope lock: *"campaign creation, management, or reporting"* only. Google has no jurisdiction over WhatsApp messaging.

The real exposure is **advertiser-side policy**, which hits (a) our sellers, and (b) **iGrowFast itself if igrowfast.com ever runs Google Ads**:
- [Unacceptable business practices](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/15938071): *"Scamming people by hiding or misrepresenting info about your business, products or services isn't allowed. You can't offer products or services that you don't have or can't deliver."* Prohibited: *"Enticing users to part with money or information through a fictitious business that lacks the qualifications or capacity to provide the advertised products or services"*; *"Providing an inaccurate business name or business name that does not clearly represent the advertised business."* Enforcement is brutal: *"your Google Ads accounts will be suspended upon detection and without prior warning, and you will not be allowed to advertise with Google Ads again."*
- [Misrepresentation](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6020955) and [Dishonest pricing practices](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/15938375): *"Failure to clearly and conspicuously disclose the payment model or full expense that a user will bear."*
- [Business information requirements](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/12499303) and [Advertiser verification](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/9703665): Google verifies advertiser legal identity and **displays the verified legal name and country in the ad's "About this advertiser"** disclosure.

**Direct hit on the entity strategy:** the "US company" positioning against Morocco-centric operations and German infrastructure. Google Ads API's own docs do not police this. But advertiser verification will surface "iGrowFast LLC / United States" publicly if we advertise, and "inaccurate business name that does not clearly represent the advertised business" is an *egregious* violation with permanent ban and no warning. Since iGrowFast LLC is a genuine Wyoming entity and the site would be its own, that verification is truthful. The risk is not the entity — it's **marketing copy that overstates US-ness or implies capacity/qualifications we lack**. Keep copy factual.

## WHERE THINGS LAND — SUMMARY

**Marketing website (igrowfast.com):**
- Integrations page: text-only "Google Ads™", "Google Analytics™", "Google Sheets™" with adjective+generic construction. No Google logos unless a permission request is filed and granted.
- Trademark notice line (footer or integrations page): "Google Ads™, Google Analytics™ and Google Sheets™ are trademarks of Google LLC. iGrowFast LLC is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Google LLC."
- Live, functioning, describing the real tool — **hard prerequisite for the token application itself**.
- Privacy policy (public URL).
- No "partner/official/powered by Google" anywhere.

**In-app (app.igrowfast.com):**
- Google Analytics logo permitted under the GA developer branding policy, must link back to Google Analytics, not the most prominent element, min sizes respected.
- No replication of Google Ads UI look and feel.
- >24h data-delay disclosure if applicable.
- MB scoping enforced server-side.

**Customer contract (Terms / DPA):**
- Written consent for MB access to Google Ads account data.
- Statement that iGrowFast accesses the customer's Google Ads / Analytics / Sheets on their authorization.
- 3-business-day disassociation right.
- Fee disclosure if any management fee exists.

**Application / config (not website):**
- API Center: developer token, permissible use = **Reporting**, Basic Access, monitored contact email, accept T&C.
- Optional Cloud project brand verification (speeds review).
- Demo account provisioning capability (7-day SLA).
- Token activity ≥ once per 90 days.
- Google Brand Permission Request Form — only if logos are wanted.

requirements.where_it_lands: App: campaign report UI design. Website: visual design must not imitate Google trade dress.

requirements.requirement: Must provide a demo account to the API tool within 7 days of a Google request — live or functionally identical. A false account is a violation. Standard Access additionally requires being ready to provide demo sign-in access. Maintain a permanently working demo login.
requirements.where_it_lands: Operational/config: standing demo account on app.igrowfast.com + monitored API contact inbox (compliance team contacts it during review).

requirements.requirement: Token is revoked after 90 consecutive days of inactivity. Keep a scheduled call alive once approved.
requirements.where_it_lands: Config: cron/keepalive on the Google Ads API client.

requirements.requirement: Google Analytics logo MAY be used without special approval by apps that display GA data publicly, to non-owners, or commercially (this describes the per-MB GA surfacing exactly). Conditions: logo must link back to Google Analytics; min 154x50px horizontal / 132x100px vertical; never the most prominent element; no modifying/altering/covering; cannot use 'Google Analytics' in the app's primary name or description. Approved phrasing: 'works with Google Analytics'. Note the policy's scope is 'within an application' — for the marketing site, text-only is the zero-risk read.
requirements.where_it_lands: App: GA data views may carry the linked GA logo. Website: prefer text-only.

requirements.requirement: Google Sheets naming on the marketing site: 'for Google Sheets™', 'for use with Google Sheets™', 'compatible with Google Sheets™' are the explicitly permitted constructions. Do not use Google brand elements as the app logo. Standard, unaltered screenshots of Google services are permitted for illustration — but any Sheets screenshot must contain zero real end-customer PII.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website: integrations page copy + any screenshot assets.

requirements.requirement: Data security: 'You must use all reasonable efforts to keep advertisers' Google Ads API data in a secure environment at all times', per commonly acceptable security standards; all transfers require at least 128-bit SSL encryption. Note: there is NO retention/deletion period in the Ads API T&C — the only deletion duty is of API Specifications at termination (Sec 15). Do not draft a policy claiming a Google-mandated Ads retention period.
requirements.where_it_lands: Config/infrastructure: TLS on api.igrowfast.com (already via Cloudflare Tunnel) + box hardening. Contract: security clause.

requirements.requirement: NO Google policy restricts COD, dropshipping, or automated messaging for an Ads API tool. The API's only use restriction is 'You can only use the Google Ads API for Google Ads campaign creation, management, or reporting.' The real exposure is advertiser-side: if igrowfast.com itself advertises on Google Ads, Unacceptable Business Practices bans 'an inaccurate business name that does not clearly represent the advertised business' and 'enticing users ... through a fictitious business that lacks the qualifications or capacity to provide the advertised products or services' — egregious, suspension on detection without warning, permanent ban. Advertiser verification will publicly display the verified legal name and country. iGrowFast LLC is a genuine WY entity so verification is truthful; the risk is marketing copy overstating US-ness or capacity.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website: marketing copy must stay factual about the entity and capability. Non-website: advertiser verification filing if/when running Google Ads.

requirements.requirement: Third-party transparency: be honest and transparent about company, services, associated costs and expected results. If a management fee is charged, inform new customers in writing before each first purchase and disclose it on all invoices. Provide customer IDs on request. Monthly performance report with cost/clicks/impressions at Google account level, OR let customers sign in to their own Google account directly (the latter satisfies it).
requirements.where_it_lands: Contract + invoices + billing flow. Website: pricing page must be honest about fees.

requirements.requirement: Google Workspace Marketplace listing — FUTURE ONLY, not currently applicable. The Sheets sync uses a service account (server-to-server), which is not a Marketplace app and triggers no OAuth consent screen. If ever rebuilt as a user-OAuth add-on and listed: billing enabled on the GCP project; app review (design, content, functionality, UX); OAuth verification as a SEPARATE process with possible demo video; annual third-party security assessment if restricted scopes. Sheets scopes are sensitive not restricted, so verification yes / annual assessment likely no. Recommendation: do not go to Marketplace.
requirements.where_it_lands: Future application path only. No website impact today.

requirements.requirement: Brand verification of Google Cloud projects is 'optional and is used only as a signal for faster determination of Ads API Basic Access eligibility.' Worth doing to expedite the ~5 business day review.
requirements.where_it_lands: Config: Google Cloud console OAuth branding. Not a website item.

requirements.requirement: Cloud-managed access levels (developer-token-free path) is a PILOT with limited availability and still requires an already-approved developer token plus a Google Cloud organization. Not a shortcut around the application.
requirements.where_it_lands: Future config option only.
